transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it’s a bit of a long story, I suppose. I've been volunteering with the local historical society for a few years now, just to keep busy since I haven't been working, you know? But recently... well, what brings me in is this whole situation with our spring fundraiser. I just sort of took the entire project on like I could run the whole thing myself. 

I mean, usually we have a committee of five or six people to handle these things, but I just felt this absolute rush of inspiration and took complete control. I started drawing up all these elaborate quilt designs for an auction—I had this vision for a whole series based on the town's founding families, so I was up sketching those out, and then I was calling every single volunteer on our roster. I was on the phone constantly, making these huge, detailed schedules for everyone, mapping out every hour of the event and who needed to be where. And I ended up promising the board all these strict deadlines that... well, looking at it now, there was just no earthly way I couldn't possibly meet them. There are only twenty-four hours in a day, after all! But at the time, I just felt so incredibly capable, like I could organize the whole county if I needed to, and I just kept piling more and more on my plate until the whole thing just spiraled completely out of hand.
Have you ever had a period, lasting days or weeks, where you felt unusually low, sad, or lacking energy and interest, either before this or at any other time in your life?

Well, yes. Yes, I have. It’s actually... well, it’s quite distressing, to be perfectly honest with you, because it's such a stark contrast to how I was just describing myself. Normally, I like to think of myself as a very engaged person, but I do get these stretches—and they really can last for weeks, just dragging on and on—where it’s like someone just pulled the plug right out of the wall. 

Take my hobbies, for instance. I used to absolutely love checking on my garden. I have these raised beds out back—mostly vegetables, some beautiful heirloom tomatoes, a few rows of zinnias and marigolds to keep the pests away—and I’d be out there every single morning with my cup of coffee, just inspecting every little leaf and pulling weeds before they could even take root. And the same goes for my sewing. Not the historical society projects, mind you, but my own personal quilt entries for the county fair. I would normally spend hours and hours matching colors and planning these intricate geometric patterns. 

But lately... well, when I get into one of these slumps, I just can't bring myself to care about any of it. The mail carrier will drop off the new spring seed catalogs, or those beautiful, thick glossy fabric catalogs from the quilting shop down in the valley, and I’ll just leave them sitting right there in a pile on the kitchen table. I just look at the fabric swatches and the pictures of the plants and I feel... nothing much at all. It’s just this heavy, flat feeling where all my enthusiasm usually is, and I just sit there at the table wondering why I can't even muster a drop of interest for the things that usually bring me so much joy. It's like the color just completely drains out of my day-to-day life.

During that time when you felt so capable and were taking on the fundraiser, did you experience anything unusual—like hearing voices others couldn't hear, or having beliefs that others found strange or told you weren't true?

Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I mean, I know sometimes people can get sort of carried away and imagine things, but my mind was perfectly grounded in reality, at least as far as what was actually happening around me. I certainly wasn't hearing voices or anything out of the ordinary like that. To be perfectly honest, the only voices I was hearing were the ones on the telephone, because like I said, I was calling absolutely everyone in the county directory! 

I remember I called Martha Higgins—she’s been our treasurer for, oh, it must be fifteen years now, ever since her husband retired from the savings and loan—and I called her at maybe six-thirty in the morning to discuss the budget for the auction centerpieces. Now, she definitely thought my timing was strange, and she told me in no uncertain terms that I was being entirely unrealistic about how much we could accomplish in just three weeks. She kept saying, "You can't possibly sew that many quilts by yourself," but it wasn't because she thought I was having bizarre, made-up beliefs. It was just because I was trying to do the work of ten people all by myself. 

I never thought I had magical powers or anything like that, or that someone was sending me secret messages. It was really just this overwhelming sense of... well, capability, like I mentioned before. I just felt like I had finally woken up and had all the energy in the world to get our historical society the funding it desperately needed for the roof repairs on the old schoolhouse building. We've been trying to fix those shingles since the big storm two winters ago. So, no, no voices, no strange beliefs... just a very, very unrealistic schedule and a whole lot of overconfidence.

During that period when you felt so capable and energetic, did it cause serious problems in your daily life—such as conflicts with others, financial trouble, or needing to be hospitalized—or did it require any intervention to stop you from continuing?

Well, yes, it... it really did cause quite a bit of trouble, though maybe not in the way of going to a hospital or anything like that. But it made an absolute mess of my real life. My poor husband—he’s been an absolute saint through all of this, bless his heart. I mean, normally I run a very tight ship here at home. I have my routines, I do the grocery shopping on Tuesdays to avoid the crowds, I keep the house tidy, I make sure dinner is sorted out... but well, he has had to completely take over all the household routines. The cooking, the laundry, even just remembering to bring the trash bins down to the curb, because I just completely dropped the ball on my end. 

And then there’s the historical society, which is just... oh, it’s just mortifying to even think about. Because I had made all those elaborate promises, right? I had all these people waiting on me for the quilt designs and the schedules and the auction materials. But when it all became too much and the reality of what I'd taken on finally hit me, I just... I stopped keeping my commitments entirely. The deadlines came and went, and I just couldn't do it. I couldn't even bring myself to face the people who were waiting on me. I couldn't bear to look Martha or the board members in the eye after making such a huge fuss and promising them the moon. 

So my husband has actually had to deal with the historical society for me, too. He’s had to field the phone calls, go down there, and basically untangle the massive web I spun, just to explain that I wouldn't be able to deliver on anything I said I would. It’s so terribly embarrassing, having your husband step in to manage your volunteer friends and apologize on your behalf, all because you’re too ashamed to even answer the telephone when they call to ask where the things you promised them are.

This episode caused marked functional impairment (husband had to take over household and social/volunteer obligations), consistent with a full manic episode rather than hypomania. No psychotic features (hallucinations/delusions) were present, ruling out F31.2. She also reports distinct past/separate episodes of depressed mood with anhedonia (loss of interest in gardening and quilting) lasting weeks, confirming a bipolar course rather than a single manic episode (ruling out F30.x). Therefore, the current presentation is Bipolar disorder, current episode manic without psychotic symptoms (F31.1).
